newsitem.title: UK: UK's David Smith first half strong but sounds warning.
newsitem.headline: UK's David Smith first half strong but sounds warning.

text.p: British packaging and paper firm David S. Smith Plc on Wednesday posted interim profits at the top of market forecasts but warned that poor trading conditions in the rest of Europe would hit second half earnings.
The company reported pre-tax profits of 58.6 million pounds ($96.91 million) for the first half ended November 2, down from 59.6 million pounds in the year-ago period.
The results topped most analysts' expectations, which ranged from 52.0 to 58.0 million pounds.
However, the firm warned that strength in the pound and continued weakness in the French and German economies would cause second-half earnings to fall below its interim results.
Chief executive Peter Williams said the last six months of the year were normally the company's strongest half.

"This means that when we say we're less (in the forthcoming second half), it's actually more of a reduction in profits than a straight (year-ago) comparison would have given," he told Reuters in an interview.
He added that the company expected poor trading conditions to continue into the first half of next financial year, although he declined to give earnings estimates for that period.
"I'm not about to make a forecast, but I think you can surmise from that that it's unlikely to be at this year's (first half) level," he said.
The company's shares tumbled after the profit warning, dropping 18 pence to 288.5 by 1040 GMT.
"The company's performed very resiliently. But it's a very cautious statement, and that was a bit of a surprise," said a paper analyst who asked not to be named.
"The stock fell more than what we expected, but from this level, we would certainly be buyers," he added, noting the company's strong management and good long-term prospects.
The company said it was pleased with its first-half performance, given the weakness in continental Europe, where it has about one-third of its operations.

"At a time when the Continent is flat and many of our competitors have extra capacity and are looking to export, the fact that the UK economy is strong and has a strong currency gives them lots of encouragement," Williams said.
He added that the recent truckers' strike that crippled the French economy also hurt the company's November results, though not significantly.
"It just adds to an already pretty black scene," he said.
He was cautious about predicting when the company would see a recovery in its markets.
"I have no doubt that we'll see a recovery by '98, but whether it's earlier is another issue," he said.
Williams said the company did not plan any large cost-cutting or redundancy programmes in the face of the poor trading environment.
"We don't change the way we operate because of the ebb and flow of markets. We are constantly looking at cost-cutting, and we are constantly looking to improve our operations," he said.
